subtopic: MOTION URGING ALL POSSIBLE EFFORTS TO PROMOTE DECENTRALIZATION
MOTION URGING ALL POSSIBLE EFFORTS TO PROMOTE DECENTRALIZATION
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of taking advantage of every possible opportunity to promote the decentralization of industry, particularly with reference to defence industry, thereby,
(1)	helping to reverse the trend towards concentration of population in large metropolitan areas with the accompanying social evils;
(2)	encouraging a more equitable distribution of population and development right across Canada, and
(3)	assuring the strategic dispersal of vital war industries in the interests of national defence.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is three years since I first placed this motion on the order paper. In previous years we have exhausted the number of days allotted to private members before arriving at this particular resolution. But in the interval I have been interested to notice that a good many of the resolutions that are placed before this house from time to time by members in various parties relate to the implications of the resolution that we have before us today, that is, the desirability of decentralization

and diversification of industry for the general well-being of national development in Canada.
At the very outset, Mr. Speaker, I would emphasize that I am speaking not only in terms of decentralization as between regions. I also wish to emphasize, right at the beginning, that there is a desirability of decentralization and diversification within the various provinces themselves. I raise that point because in this country it is quite obvious that there is the general tendency for the few large urban centres that we have-the half dozen or so large metropolitan communities-to become increasingly larger at the expense of the smaller communities across the country.
Even though we have been delayed somewhat in time in coming to this resolution, it seems to me that it has become more important as time goes on. Since the war we have been passing through a post-war boom. All the experts in economics are now quite free in acknowledging that we have passed through this transition period of post-war adjustment which, from the standpoint of Canada, might be described as an economic honeymoon. We have been placed in an extremely favourable position in relation to the economies of other countries. But that honeymoon is now past and the fact of the situation is that we must face the economic realities if we are to continue to progress as we have during recent years.
Unfortunately, during the transition period the tendency for industry to concentrate in the two central provinces and in the larger urban areas has been intensified rather than decreased and today we are faced with a situation-to sum it up in general terms- where 60 per cent of the population, 80 per cent of the manufacturing and 50 per cent of the total mineral production is concentrated in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. We therefore have a concentration of industry, population and-what is perhaps more important so far as our activities in this house are concerned-political power. The latter is perhaps one of the most significant features of this trend that has been noted.
The Gordon commission has been meeting across Canada within recent months and I have followed with a great deal of interest the press summaries of the various briefs presented to this important commission. In every province-particularly those in the maritimes and in the prairie region-without exception the briefs have emphasized the necessity of carrying out the principle of
Decentralization of Industry the resolution we have before us. For example, the brief from the Manitoba government expressed the need in these terms:
Decentralization of industry is essential to a sound national economy and it is imperative that steps be taken and programs developed which will ensure the spreading out of industries throughout Canada.
That is the official viewpoint of the Manitoba government. I was especially interested to note the other day the brief presented by the joint labour groups, namely the Canadian Congress of Labour and the Trades and Labour Congress. They went right back to first principles so far as this equitable economic development of Canada is concerned, and they did so in the following words:
Nothing in the confederation debates is clearer than that the Fathers intended and expected that confederation should benefit all parts of the new nation. They would have repudiated instantly and with horror any idea that one province, one region or a group of provinces or regions should progress while the others stood still or fell back.
That is taking us right back to the first principles upon which this country was established. Perhaps from time to time it is necessary to go back to consider all the complex factors that were involved at the time of confederation. Certainly it was the vision of Sir John A. Macdonald and Georges Cartier that they would build a country strong and free from the Atlantic to the Pacific. To this end they adopted a national policy to help build a strong and democratic economy to accomplish what was considered in their day an almost impossible task, and even in the light of contemporary engineering capacity is still regarded as a tremendous engineering feat, the construction of the Canadian Pacific right through to the west coast.
Since that time we have tended to lose sight of the problems Canada was up against in the launching of this federal experiment. More recently in Canadian public affairs the necessity for development on a national scale has become somewhat obscured by the game of regional politics. The west has been played off against the east, and as a result of economic frustration the west has gone splintering off in various political directions. I think, Mr. Speaker, that the time has come, as has been underlined by the recent activities of the Gordon commission, for a serious re-appraisal of economic policies in the light of Canada's great position and power as a nation in world affairs. If it was important at the beginning of Canada's national existence to the development of this unique experiment in sovereignty in the northern part of the North American continent, it is even more imperative now in view of the much more important position that Canada occupies in international affairs.

Decentralization of Industry
It will be noted, Mr. Speaker, that the resolution is divided into three parts. It refers not only to the general principle of decentralization, but also we have enlarged on that particular aspect and have broken it down into three of the more important facets that are involved in carrying out this principle. First of all, there is the tendency for industry and population to concentrate in small regional areas, particularly urban areas. This has been one of the most characteristic phenomena of the last 100 years in the western world. We have seen the development of the factory system, which emerged out of the industrial revolution. Because of the large amount of labour involved in factory industry there has been an influx of workers, an influx of population from the rural areas to the urban areas, and that is a process that has continued up until recent times. Out of this concentration of population in urban areas there has been a growth in social problems which, down through the past hundred years, it has been almost impossible to cope with by government on all levels as well as by private agencies of various kinds. Indeed, there is a general feeling that uncontrolled urbanization, unplanned urbanization, has given rise to some of the extreme social problems that we are still confronted with in Canada as well as in other western countries.
Characteristic of urban growth has been the emergence of slums, blighted areas, within the heart of our large industrial cities. In Canada we obviously are still trying to cope with the problem of slums in the big cities, because just the other day we had placed before the house by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) some further attempts to deal with the problem of slum control, and that is merely the physical manifestation of the problem. The underlying social difficulties are much more damaging to our way of life.
In the city we have people operating largely on an impersonal level. The close relationship of the neighbourhood, which is characteristic of the rural social situation, breaks down and there tends to be an atomization of individuals. They live as separate entities in many cases. This can be demonstrated by the indices relating to symptoms of social disorganization. In many instances human beings become less than human. In the big, booming, pushing confusion of our large urban areas there is a tendency for values to change. Individuals crowded together in this situation, instead of finding satisfaction on the spiritual and intellectual level, tend to be largely motivated by physical impulses. There is all sorts of evidence in this regard; the rapid increase in commercial recreation; the


rapid increase in the consumption of alcoholic beverages. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) had some returns tabled within recent days, as recorded on page 1738 of Hansard, which indicated-I do not have to give the figures-that the consumption of alcoholic beverages has increased at a very rapid rate within recent years. I venture to say that had we the information we would see that the consumption in urban areas is much above that in rural areas. In other words, people wishing to escape from the confusion of the city do so by means of the cup that cheers.
Related to this problem of the effect upon individuals in the modern, big, booming cities, we have the impact upon the basic social institutions of the nation-and the nation is strong only in so far as the basic social institutions are strong-the family, the church, the school, and so forth. I merely emphasize the family in passing because it is the most important. No society can be great, no society can progress unless the dignity and the integrity of the family are preserved.
In the city we are constantly hearing about the problem of juvenile delinquency, the increasing divorce rate and similar evidences of family disorganization of that kind. The family in the cities, in many instances, instead of being the healing place of the soul, as it should be, the place where personality is moulded, the place where we acquire our values, the place where conscience is formed; instead of performing these functions adequately, tends to become a place of tension, disorganization and confusion. Evidence of that development again could be put forward in the statistics relating to mental illness in this country. I had a return from the Department of National Health and Welfare in this regard just a few days ago. It is dated Tuesday, February 14, 1956. It shows that in every province in Canada between the years 1950 and 1954 the admissions to our mental institutions have doubled. In 1950, the total was 16,411; in 1954, it was 29,351.
Just to carry this particular line of thought one step farther, the country has been shocked within recent weeks-in fact, we have had the subject raised in this house on several occasions by hon. members from the communities affected-by the upsurge in sexual deviation, another problem in the disorganized and confused atmosphere of the big urban community. Values become so distorted that we wonder today what is normal in the city. We rub shoulders with criminal types, with bohemian types of all kinds, and

we are completely oblivious of the fact because personalities remain largely anonymous, unknown to one another. We are completely unaware who the man right next to us might be.
When these tragedies occur there is a great outcry and particularly when the psychopath-because these persons are nothing more or less than psychopathic people who, because of the confusion in the home and so forth, have not developed a social conscience that can conform with the values of our way of life-when the psychopath, indulging in deviation, commits murder attempting to hide his deed and satisfy his twisted conscience. These are all evidences of the problem and I say it is one of the difficulties that underlie the problem, this tendency for population to concentrate in large cities; because of the very nature of industrial development the populations concentrate in large urban areas.
The government has moved slowly to do something about the social problems emerging out of this concentration. Up until 1929 very little attention was paid to the social difficulties that followed in the wake of the industrial revolution. One of the pioneers in this regard was the late Mr. Woodsworth, who was active in the city of Winnipeg during world war I when the industrial revolution first hit that community, and it was aggravated by the rapid influx of waves of immigrants, with the resultant social difficulties. That situation made its impression upon the social conscience of Mr. Woodsworth, who was a clergyman, and he became very active in agitating for reforms. In fact, I believe he was one of the pioneers in founding the social welfare council in Canada. He also later became involved in politics, as is well known, and I do not know whether or not that was a good thing for one of his convictions.
It was in 1929 with the onset of the depression that the government of Canada was forced to take action. Prior to that time we had acted according to the tenets of laissez-faire liberalism and hoped everything would adjust and regulate itself automatically for the best of all concerned. The first comprehensive attempt to cope with the problem was the new deal of Mr. R. B. Bennett passed in 1935 which did not get very far because of the vagaries of politics in this country at that time. Since that time these new measures have found their way to the statute books of Canada.
I want to make this point. All that governments can do both on the federal and provincial level is try to absorb the shocks by means of grants in aid, whether they be to government departments or to individuals

Much of our government's social welfare legislation has been in the form of financial welfare trying to bolster the economic situation of the individual caught in the disorganization of a changing society. That helps of course but it does not get down to the basic problem. The basic problem is the disorganization of our social institutions and the effect this has on personality and the development of citizens of mature stature in a democratic society.
The institutions that are really doing the job and are really getting to the heart of the matter are the churches. The basic function of the church is to provide meaning and motivation to the people in a particular nation. For example, in order to restore stability to the family unit we have heard this theme for the past few years, "The family that prays together stays together". That seems to me to go to the heart of this problem that has grown out of urban concentration in Canada.
We also have all sorts of new professions, social workers, psychiatrists, criminologists and marriage counsellors. We also have the work of the labour unions, chambers of commerce and farm organizations which endeavour to cope with the underlying difficulty. It is quite significant too that the entire service club movement has emerged within the last 30 or 40 years in this country. These are the groups which are getting down to the basic problem.
One association which I think is really coming to the heart of the matter so far as the approach we are taking in this resolution is concerned, and that is the decentralization of industry, is the Canadian community planning association which has an active organization right across the country in every province. The Canadian community planning association is dealing with the problem of concentration in urban areas. It is endeavouring to plan communities in such a way that the social and traffic problems which are so besetting us today will be solved. We also have our own national capital plan which will attempt to unravel some of the mistakes of the past over the course of the next few decades.
One of the essential measures of the community planning association is to restore the neighbourhood atmosphere wherein people can recover the feeling of belonging to a closely knit group of fellow humans. It is trying to meet the need and the desire that

Decentralization of Industry lies deep in every one of us to have a rose-covered garden by developing green belt areas where a neighbourhood atmosphere can be restored.
The emphasis of all these voluntary groups is towards the decentralization and relocation of the Canadian population on a more equitable basis throughout these wide open spaces to which we have fallen heir. If we are going to accomplish that it means, of course, that there must be a decentralization of industry. Manufacturing, secondary industry, is a large user of labour today. If we are going to be able to restore our urban communities it means that we have to get the population out of the centre of these communities. We have to scatter industry on a much broader geographic basis.
I admit at once that everybody talks about this. As I look through the resolutions that are still before the house I find they relate themselves very closely to this subject. The subject of decentralization is almost like the subject of the weather; everybody talks about it but no one does anything to change it. I will admit further that it is an extremely difficult project to carry out particularly where you have to .go against the laws of economics such as the tendency for industries to congregate together for the sake of mutual support.
At this point I wish to go back to the first principle I enunciated at the outset of my remarks. In the past we had to fly in the face of economic reality for the sake in the first instance of establishing this country and later for preserving its sovereign strength as a nation in the midst of challenging circumstances, originally from south of the border, and then later involvement in two world wars. Therefore I suggest that something more than economic factors must be considered if we are going to deal with this problem.
I do not intend to merely talk about this subject; I have one or two specific suggestions which over the long-run period will, I feel, help to bring about a greater degree of decentralization of industry. The tragedy is that the trend has all been in the other direction. Instead of the situation becoming easier through the passing of time the concentration has been aggravated in recent years. That is perhaps why we in less populous regions make so much noise about it in this house. If there were evident a reversal of the trend, perhaps we would be mollified to a certain extent.
First of all, and I merely mention this subject in passing, it has become obvious during recent weeks in this house that western agriculture is in a declining position. We [iur. Dinsdale.]

had some three weeks' discussion on this subject so I do not feel obliged to reiterate the points that were made. Because of the revolution that is taking place in agriculture through mechanization and other causes, we see a condition of a declining population in rural areas. For example, in 1921 40 per cent of the labour force in Manitoba was occupied in agriculture whereas in 1951 only 24 per cent of the total labour force in that province was occupied in agriculture. That means that our ability to absorb and employ people in agriculture is declining.
That is one reason why the prairie regions, with the great spaces they possesss, have not been able to participate fully in the immigration program which has been carried on since the war. A most disappointing percentage of the newcomers have settled on the prairies. The only way we can provide employment for newcomers is to have an opportunity to industrialize. The only way we can prevent this migration from the rural areas which is still going on is to have a diversified industrial program on the prairies. We must consider the position of agriculture as the first point.
Second, our trade policy is a most important factor in this difficulty. In Canada we have been shifting from a United Kingdom to a United States market emphasis. This has resulted in the United States having more and more influence and control in our Canadian economy. Because of the high level of development of the United States economy and the great market they provide for mass raw material exports, we find we have been exporting an astounding amount of newsprint, minerals and metals in recent years. I do not have to harp on this point because it is obvious that if we are going to emerge into a position of strength population-wise, and in financial and industrial terms that our position in world affairs calls for, we must get away from economic primitivism and move more and more toward exerting some of that vision which was exerted at the time of confederation. We must get into secondary industrial activities. If we want to express it in original terms, we must apply some of this national policy to western Canada and the maritimes-they will speak for themselves later on I trust-that was applied by Sir John Macdonald to central Canada at the beginning of the life of this nation.
Then there is the matter of our petroleum industry and the possibility of decentralization. We are going to be considering in this house shortly an important measure, the trans-Canada pipeline, and it is hoped, speaking from the western viewpoint, that gas will be sold at the minimum economic

price. Unless that is done we are not going to enjoy the special benefits which the possession of this form of energy should give to western Canada. Unfortunately many important projects have been delayed because of the delay in getting under way with this activity.
There is a taxation feature which should be considered by the federal government. Canadian oil companies are at a disadvantage in competing with United States firms in the Canadian oil field because of the less advantageous position our Canada oil people occupy in comparison with their United States counterparts. The United States government gives special incentives to such an extent that much of the United States risk capital operating in the Canadian financial market is made up of money saved because of the absence of excessive taxation. That government also gives a more generous allowance for depletion.
From another standpoint transportation is important to the prairie west, particularly to Manitoba, because we stand mid-way. Under the topic of transportation I should like to include briefly the subject of highways. The federal government is moving slowly and cautiously into the area of highway construction by its grants in aid to the trans-Canada highway. That is a beginning which we in Manitoba feel will have to go much further. Considering the matter from the standpoint of national defence requirements, the opportunities offered by the tourist industry and the provision of access to our natural resources, it seems to us that the federal government will have to take a much more active hand in developing a suitable highway system than it has up to the present time. It has large returns from excise taxes on automobiles, petroleum products and so forth and that money could not be put to better use than in the development of a highway system in the interests of the general development of Canada.
We are interested also in the St. Lawrence seaway and we give hearty approval to that measure because it is going to improve the transportation situation in Canada. But if the people of Manitoba as well as those in other sections of the prairies are to benefit, certain factors will have to be kept in mind. It must be remembered that the terminal facilities at the head of the lakes are not adequate to deal with the larger vessels which will be coming through. The harbour facilities will have to be deepened. Unless these problems are taken care of in the over-all planning of the St. Lawrence seaway there will be no direct benefit to the prairie economy.
Decentralization of Industry The highway from the head of the lakes to Winnipeg is going to be totally inadequate according to present standards as soon as the seaway is put through and the head of the lakes becomes the busy seaport it is anticipated it will be.
Then there is the problem of air transportation in the west. On a per capita basis the people of Manitoba use air transport more than the people of any other area in Canada. We were disappointed when the application of Canadian Pacific Air Lines for a through freight franchise was turned down. That works to the disadvantage of Manitoba. We were disappointed also when Winnipeg, which now has an international airport, was denied the privilege of passenger rights on the line operating from the west coast to Europe.
These are just indications of the subtle discrimination that exists against the less populous regions. They are also evidence of the active role which the federal government can play. It is just the accumulation of these small things which will have to be overcome.
We are always interested in freight rates, and in this connection I should like to mention a little difficulty which we ran into in my own constituency. In-transit or stopover rates are not permitted in Canada, other than on grain. We have a little industry employing some 60 people operating in a small town fabricating west coast lumber into laminated structures. Because of the present freight differential they find it most difficult to compete in the eastern markets. A stopover privilege or an in-transit rate would make it possible to fabricate that lumber and ship it without any undue freight disadvantage. The industry would then be competitive in the east. Fortunately they are able to use truck transportation to save the situation at the moment, but if the pressure is continued this industry will be forced out of business.

Thank you very much for your courtesy in this regard, Mr. Speaker. I wish to raise two more points and I shall do so as briefly as I can. I have emphasized the role that government might play in this process and I would just like to mention the role that private industry is playing.
The movement of branch plants to the west is already well under way. There is a large

Decentralization of Industry enough domestic market now to provide sufficient business for an economic location of a branch plant of the larger plants with headquarters in eastern Canada. I should like to give one illustration of outstanding success in this regard. We have a very thriving electrical manufacturing industry that was established by four young engineers who broke away from the larger industrial firms, General Electric, Westinghouse, Great Northern and so forth. They saw an opportunity for industrial development on the prairies in the rural electrification that is going on. They pooled their talents, developed an excellent transformer and a mechanical circuit breaker, and succeeded in capturing the prairie market for rural electrification, and they are also well into the Ontario market and making headway in the Quebec market.
That is the sort of thing that is taking place from the standpoint of private initiative and private enterprise, and we should not ignore that particular development. It should be encouraged in every way, so far as tax concessions are concerned. It is difficult to get equity capital for these small firms. We must always keep in mind that over 75 per cent of Canadian employing firms have less than 15 employees, and they are the nucleus around which the other industrial developments will grow that will make Canada the strong nation industrially and economically we know she is destined to be.
Now for one final point. This is the matter of defence industries. I could not let this subject pass entirely without mentioning that recently General Worthington, who is in charge of civil defence, has been talking about the need for decentralized population. He makes the claim that no city should have more than 50,000 people. He goes further and says that it should not have more than 50,000 people even if there were no threat from hydrogen bomb warfare. His reasoning is that once a city grows beyond that level it runs into the social problems that I outlined at the outset of my remarks.
The field of defence industries is one area where government should participate directly, and certainly with a great deal more enthusiasm than it has in any period of emergency. During world war II we in the west were depopulated because of the rush of the population to the factories in the east. It has been little better during the Korean episode. We find most of our defence industries, in fact all of them, concentrated in the two large urban areas of Montreal and Toronto. I do not have to labour that point. It is obvious in this day of the threat of the H-bomb that if we are going to have any reasonable and sensible defence program at all, basic to that 

program should be the decentralization and the relocation of at least our defence industries.

subtopic: MOTION URGING ALL POSSIBLE EFFORTS TO PROMOTE DECENTRALIZATION
speechtext:
I have listened with great interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris, the sponsor of this resolution. I think he mentioned that possibly members from the maritimes might wish to speak on behalf of their part of the country, and that is my intention to a considerable extent.
It is my thought that in this debate we should consider first the general principle of the decentralization of Canadian industry, which is, I think, the core of the whole resolution; and then the possibilities of a practical application of such a principle, particularly with regard to the nature and scope of the role that the federal government might properly and legitimately play in relation thereto. It seems to me that in connection with the first object of our consideration, which of course is more general, there are not as many difficulties arising as in the case of the second.
The term "decentralization of industry'* may, I suppose, be applied either to a national decentralization-that is, a wider distribution of industry generally over the whole country-or merely to, shall I say, an intra-provincial decentralization, which would be a spreading of industry within the boundaries of one particular province. If I understand the hon. member for Brandon-Souris correctly, he said that his remarks were intended to be applicable, to some extent at least, to both types of decentralization. In this regard,
I note that in the present resolution there are listed three objectives, as I might call them. Summarizing them somewhat, I would say that these are indicated as being attainable through a decentralization of industry: a less pronounced metropolitan concentration of people; a more equitable distribution of population and development right across Canada; and, third, a strategic dispersal of war industries.
In view of the vast geographical expanse of the provinces where Canadian industry is, and where, unfortunately, it shows all too many signs of continuing to be, largely concentrated, a merely intra-provincial decentralization of industry might constitute at least a partial step toward the attainment of the first and third objectives mentioned in the resolution. That is not so, however, as regards the second objective; for any results in that quarter, only a national decentralization would be effective.
It might be pointed out, in so far as an intraprovincial decentralization is concerned, this government and this parliament would,

:it seems to me, have comparatively little concern with that type. Only national decentralization, as I have defined it, is really entitled to the status of a national problem. I take it this resolution is intended to apply, at least primarily, to such national decentralization. In any event, I should like to say that in so far as my own remarks are concerned, when I refer hereafter to the decentralization of industry, I am thinking in terms of what I have called national decentralization, such as would affect the dominion as a whole and not merely one or two provinces.
It must be recognized that there are many difficulties in the way of the practical application of any wide principle of decentralization, but I am convinced that the principle itself is sound and that the possibilities of promoting it by such measures as may properly lie within the federal purview are worthy of the earnest consideration of this house as offering a prospect of materially advancing the best interests of Canada as a nation. It is my opinion that a widespread decentralization of industry would promote the best interests of every part of this country. I am aware that such an opinion is likely to be received with an attitude of extreme scepticism and possibly one of downright rejection by those provinces that industrially are now pre-eminently the favoured ones of Canada.
That attitude, to my mind, is an utterly mistaken one, though perhaps not unnatural, and of that attitude I intend to speak more in a few minutes. But, in so far as decentralization means spreading industry into those provinces which now are industrially deficient, I think there is no shadow of doubt whatever that it would be of incalculable benefit to such areas. To no region in Canada is that statement more applicable, in my opinion, than it is to the maritimes. For there the lack of sound industrial development and opportunity has, I maintain, been one of the greatest handicaps, if not the greatest, which have plagued us ever since the beginning of this century.
I turn again to the three objectives-as I say, I think that is the proper term-which are listed in the present resolution. I do not think any lengthy argument is necessary to emphasize the inherent value of all three. Let us examine the first. Let us consider whether it is in any way desirable to have vast numbers of people gathered in restricted, crowded, built-up areas, and whether any real justification remains-if it ever existed- for the growth of cities which number their population in the millions.
I think perhaps I am treading on safe ground there because I do not believe either Montreal or Toronto has yet reached a plural
Decentralization of Industry figure. Whatever the answers may have been in the past, I think that today two things, namely traffic and the hydrogen bomb, provide two new and cogent negatives to the question; and that is apart altogether from the high incidence of crime, misery and general human degradation which so often characterizes the life of a really huge city.
In distant ages national populations tended to swarm together in walled cities for the purpose of making more effective defence against their enemies. In more recent centuries heavy concentrations of population in cities tended to simplify the problems of communication and transport which then existed. Of course for countries such as England or Japan, it may well be that the huge city is the inevitable and inescapable result of limited land areas and dense populations. But not one of these factors applies with any force to the Canada of today. In proportion as our cities are overgrown, they simply present the choicer targets for the hydrogen bomb in time of war and an increasingly hopeless congestion of traffic in time of peace. Certainly in this half continent of ours there is no lack of space for population dispersal if it is considered desirable that the population shall be more widely scattered.
I agree with those who advocate-and this is not a new idea

as the ideal for the conditions under which modern man must live, a wider dispersal of urban populations into comparatively scattered towns and cities of no more than moderate size. That is the ideal. In so far as the present resolution tends to encourage some progress toward that goal, I think it has a worthy aim.
Some of the observations I have just made apply with equal force to the third objective mentioned in the resolution. The destruction of a substantial proportion of our total population by means of a single hydrogen bomb dropped upon one huge city would, even apart from all humanitarian considerations, have a disastrous effect upon our will and our capacity to carry on war. Equally crippling would be the eradication of any large segment of our defence production facilities in a similar sudden manner. In case of war industries located near our cities, as unfortunately many of them are today, one single bomb might serve a dual purpose.
We are told that the duration of any future total war will be necessarily brief, a matter of a few weeks at most. No doubt that is correct. Nonetheless, any shreds of victory will certainly accrue to that side which has best preserved its people and its war-making potential. The wider dispersal of our defence
1798	HOUSE OF
Decentralization of Industry industries as well as our population would be a tangible step toward that end.
All matters pertaining to national defence are, of course, of vital concern to every Canadian from the Atlantic to the Pacific. In the maritimes, however, we face no problems, at least no serious ones, concerning the undue concentration of either people or industry. On the contrary, our lack of industrial development, with the attendant lack of opportunity for our young people, has led to a steady and continuing hemorrhage of our population to other parts of the continent. In earlier days this was chiefly to the United States, so that it is said there are more persons of Nova Scotian descent in New England than there are in their own ancestral province. In more recent times the flow has been rather toward central Canada, a change of direction which undoubtedly is beneficial in so far as Canada is concerned, but which nonetheless has upon the maritimes very much the same effect, with far too slow a rate of growth in our population.
We need more population in the maritimes, Mr. Speaker. We need more population fully as much as does any other quarter of the dominion. To achieve it I think we must have a greater development of our industrial potential. Certainly in the foreseeable future there is not the slightest danger, in so far as our part of the country is concerned, that any steps which may be taken toward attainment of these ends will lead to an undue concentration of either people or industry, such as that which already obtains in certain areas of central Canada. If anyone here should doubt that statement, all I can do is assure him that we are certainly willing to incur the risk with the utmost equanimity.
The third objective mentioned in the present resolution is to a marked degree a concomitant or perhaps one might call it a component of the broader second objective. Bearing that point in mind, I would say that from the economic point of view it is the latter which is the most significant factor of the whole resolution in so far as my part of the country is concerned. A more equitable distribution of population and development right across Canada, to use the words of the resolution, would fill a real and long-felt need in the maritime provinces. In view of what I have said, Mr. Speaker, I find myself, both from a regional and from a national standpoint, in accord with the principle of decentralization of industry as it is advocated in the present resolution.
At the outset, however, I said that after considering the principle itself, I thought we should then consider the possibilities of its
[Mr. Lusby.l

practical application, particularly with regard, to the nature and scope of the role which the federal government might legitimately and feasibly play in relation thereto.
I think it is clear that that role, even at its widest, must be subject to marked limitations. It is the aim of the federal government, of course, to maintain at all times a national economic climate favourable to industrial development and expansion. That is an aim, I may add, which has been attended with a remarkable degree of success. But the attainment of that aim does not in itself contribute to the decentralization of industry. It certainly is essential for industrial development and expansion anywhere but, as I say, it does not lead to the decentralization of industry. In fact it may perhaps be fairly said that because of the success with which that aim of general prosperity has been pursued in this country there exists today this tremendous concentration of industry in central Canada.
The federal government, of course, cannot meddle in fields of purely provincial jurisdiction or, under our system of free enterprise, compel the location of private industries in any specified area. Private industry will go where it appears most profitable to go. Consequently it seems to me that all efforts toward decentralization of industry must be directed to make it profitable for industry either to remain in or to migrate to the area which it is wished to build up.
Now, what does lie within the possible purview of the federal authority in this regard? I was interested in reading a few days ago, Mr. Speaker, of the representations with respect to the maritimes contained in the recent joint submissions of the trades and labour congress of Canada and the Canadian congress of labour to the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects, the Gordon commission. In view of the fact that maritime prosperity has advanced at a slower rate than has that of other parts of the country, the submission urged that the maritimes should be regarded as a special area. The submission did not confine itself only to the area of the maritimes, but it did urge that the martimes be regarded as a special area. They urged that, to bring industry to the workers, governments at all levels-this was not directed merely to the federal government-should adopt a four-point program consisting of tax concessions and other financial inducements to firms to remain in or go to special areas; the channeling of purchases, particularly by the dominion government, to firms in special areas; further assistance t industries through the subsidization of freight rates; and the subsidization power production in special areas.

I might add here incidentally that a number of people laid stress upon hydro and atomic power plants, but my own feeling is that the real future of electrical development in Nova Scotia is and should be directed to the development of electrical power by coal. I think that would be in the best interests of the maritime provinces. However, those four points were made in the brief. I think whatever difficulties of practical application there may be with regard to any of these proposals, they are all deserving of careful study. I hope this government will give long and sympathetic consideration to any recommendations which may emanate from the royal commission with respect to that four-point program to which I referred.
It must not be forgotten, of course, that this government is not entirely a stranger by any means to actions designed to build up industry in certain areas. For instance, this government extends a very large measure of assistance to our Nova Scotia coal industry through a system of subventions. Then again special freight rates designed to benefit maritime industry have long been in effect.
It seems to me that one promising avenue of new federal assistance to build up maritime industries, thereby furthering national decentralization of industry, might lie in the allotment of government contracts, on a preferential regional basis, to firms in the mari-times in this particular instance. In my own town of Amherst we have several industries which from time to time have been successful in obtaining orders from the federal government, particularly the Department of Defence Production. The employment thus provided has been of inestimable value, not only to the town but to the surrounding county. I believe that is an example of encouragement which can be given to industry, and to the people in an area doing vital defence work, in areas other than the highly industrialized part of the country. I might say that in particular we have in the town of Amherst a plant engaged in the manufacture of aircraft components. It seems to me that of all the industries perhaps the aircraft industry is as vital as any and is one that should be as highly decentralized as is feasible. I think a further allocation of orders to the Amherst plant, as well as further assistance in the provision of any facilities required to undertake additional government work, would be a most desirable move in the interests of such decentralization.
Some little time back, Mr. Speaker, I mentioned that a policy of decentralization of industry was unlikely to receive wholehearted support from those provinces which are now industrially in a favoured position.
Decentralization of Industry I think I said also that that was a natural but mistaken attitude. My statement was really prompted by a certain cartoon which recently appeared in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald, the work of Chambers, the inimitable staff artist of that paper. I have the cartoon here but I am not going to ask leave to table it. It is entitled, "The Geese that feed the Goose that lays the Golden Eggs", and has reference to a reported remark of the premier of Ontario that his province was Canada's goose. I understand that remark was more in connection with the fiscal arrangements which are the subject of discussion at the moment. However, I think the attitude there displayed goes much farther. The cartoon portrays our general feeling in the maritimes that Ontario lays no golden eggs for us, but on the contrary she draws from us the wherewithal to lay the eggs for herself.
If I may use another barnyard simile, I should like to say that the attitude embodied in the remark of the premier of Ontario tends to confirm a maritime suspicion that central Canada is not only the heartland but also the hogland of Canada. The latter term has no reference to the production of hogs on the farms of central Canada. It refers to those in high provincial places. That is the feeling. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that such remarks as that of the premier of Ontario give a foundation for this feeling in the less favoured parts of the country. I submit also that the attitude shown by such a remark, and it is undoubtedly shared by many others in the favoured provinces, is not only erroneous but shortsighted because in the long run the prosperity of any province of Canada is undoubtedly dependent upon a reasonable degree of prosperity being achieved throughout the rest of the country. I believe that, in turn, calls for a wider distribution of both people and industry across the whole country.
During this session there has been some talk of the possible federal role in matters of education. I should like to suggest that it might not be amiss if the federal government could devote a little effort towards attempting to educate the provincial leaders of central Canada to the truth of what I have just said.

subtopic: MOTION URGING ALL POSSIBLE EFFORTS TO PROMOTE DECENTRALIZATION
speechtext:
I welcome the opportunity to take part in this debate, Mr. Speaker. I have moved similar resolutions in this house a good many times in the past, but provoked very little discussion. I am glad to join with the prairie member from Brandon, who has now moved this resolution indicating that other parts

Decentralization of Industry of the country than the maritimes are vitally interested in the question of the decentralization of industry.
Now, to determine the value of any matter that may come before the house, one has to ask this question. Are we justified in taking up the time of the house on the subject under discussion? I think all the evidence that is available on the need for both provincial and federal governments taking a look at the concentration of industry in central Canada justifies the time we will spend on this resolution. The hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) pointed out that at the present time with respect to the dollar value of manufacturing, in the distribution and concentration of industry there is some 82 per cent in the two central provinces of Quebec and Ontario. The rest of the country has to struggle along on the other 18 per cent. I think that statement alone should bring to the mind of the federal government the necessity of taking another look at the matter of a better distribution of industry and manufacturing in order to give the country a more balanced economy, and as suggested, make for better protection in the event of war.
These considerations alone justify our discussing this resolution. The hon. member for Brandon-Souris put figures on the record, which he obtained from recent statistics, which show that 51-7 per cent of manufacturing and distribution is in the province of Ontario, and 30-3 per cent in the province of Quebec. That shows a trend toward more centralization, because as I have looked at these figures over the years I have found that they have been going up all the time. The last time I looked at them they were around 80 per cent; today they are 82 per cent.
Instead of anyone paying any attention to past discussions in the house on the question of decentralization, we find that the trend is still continuing. It may not be accidental, because this is the pattern that was followed in the United States. The United States built the centre and left the east and the west pretty much as hewers of wood and drawers of water. That influence has crept into Canada, and we are getting exactly the same development.
I want to make it quite clear that so far as the maritime members are concerned we are not suggesting there is nothing we can do for ourselves. At one time the Minister of Trade and Commerce said he was getting tired of listening to maritime members asking for handouts. We are not asking for handouts, Mr. Speaker, and I shall prove that


before I finish. I would like to impress on the minds of hon. members that what we are asking is to establish adequate industry, to have a balanced economy and to have some control over our finances. We had that in the maritime provinces before confederation.
If hon. members will take a look at a survey made by the late Norman Rogers, an economic survey of the maritimes over the past 60 years now, they will find that over 50 major industries were siphoned off from the maritimes and located in either Quebec or Ontario, many of them during my own lifetime. The late Mr. Rogers enumerated those industries. Some of them were quite large. There were cheese factories; a skate factory at Dartmouth; a sugar refinery. A nut and bolt factory, a very large one, was moved from Trenton to Montreal as late as 1946. A plate mill at Sydney was closed down and the business taken away to Ojibway, Ontario. There were many other industries. There was a fertilizer plant which was moved from Sydney; there were shoe factories. At least 50 very substantial industries, including the control of seven banks that were established before confederation, staffed and managed by Nova Scotians and mari-timers, who used their capital to finance industry and agriculture in the maritime provinces, were moved away. We are not asking the government to bring back all of these industries, but I believe that many of those that were siphoned off and centralized in the central provinces could have made just as great a contribution to the economy of Canada in the maritimes as they can in either Ontario or Quebec.
As I said before, the pattern we are following in Canada is the United States pattern. There may be a good reason for it. Maybe the United States industrialists, United States capital and citizens of the United States on Canadian boards of directors have influence enough on these boards to guide industry and investment to that part of the country to which they want it to go.
I took a look at an old file in my office just for fun today. I picked out a brief that was presented by the United Mine Workers of America to the government back in 1948. It had to do with the Nova Scotia steel industry, and on the point I am just making, the influence of Americans on Canadian corporations, they had this to say:
There is now ample evidence indicating that American interests control or may shortly control Dosco's huge steel and coal empire.
The American Securities Corporation, 25 Broad street. New York, has acquired since its formation in 1946, what we understand is a substantial interest in Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation Limited.

Mr. Charles G. Terry, president of American Securities Corporation and chairman of the finance committee of Colorado Fuel and Iron Corporation, is now a director of Dosco. Mr. R. J. Wysor, past president of Republic Steel Corporation, has also received a similar appointment to Dosco's board.
It would not seem accidental that American financial and industrial interests are acquiring an interest in one of Canada's great steel plants and deposits of high quality coal. Rather would it appear quite certain that the discovery and development of the enormously rich Quebec-Labrador iron ore field would be a fully adequate reason for American interests wishing to acquire control of Nova Scotia's two major industries, viz, steel and coal.
That statement was made back in 1948. I am not stating that they have control of the corporation, but I am suggesting that men as influential and as experienced in the fields of steel, coal and iron development could be a very large factor in influencing the development of coal, steel and iron in that particular part of the country, and maybe in other industries or in most industries in Canada. We are getting that kind of influence from the United States in developing the kind of centralized economy that we have in Canada at the present time because that is the pattern they follow in the United States.
It is rather hard to answer the question why there has not been a greater expansion of our basic steel plant. There has been some modernization, but it is creating unemployment. The investment in plant for turning out steel has increased very little since 1939. There is talk of another expansion in the production of raw steel, but I could never understand why there was not some fabrication down there. I could never understand why a modern plate mill that employed 600 people, that was established by the federal government during the war, was allowed to go out of production when 90 per cent of our steel plate is imported from the United States. That mill just petered out and was sold. I could never understand why, as recommended by the McKee report-that big company came in there and made an examination of the economy-a tin plate industry was not built around basic steel. They have the steel, the iron ore, the limestone and the coal all within a few miles of where raw steel is turned out.
I think this is a charge that no member of the government can refute. It is all right for hon. members to get on a platform or to speak on the radio or to rise in this house and say, "I am a Canadian; I am proud of Canada". Well, so am I; but you know, we have nine different kinds of Canadians in this country, and perhaps ten. There is a vast difference between the economic circumstances and the social possibilities in each of the provinces. The budget of the city of Toronto is much greater than the budget for the whole of one of the maritime provinces. When we talk about being proud of Canada, I think it should mean that we are proud of all of Canada, not of just two or three provinces.
An effort should be made to get a more balanced economy in this country. It would not take very much; you would not have to shift a great deal of industry from Ontario or Quebec to New Brunswick in order to cure the ills of that province. I am sure the Minister of Labour remembers what happened in his own riding. A textile mill at Marysville had operated for over 100 years; then the mill was closed down and the operation was shifted to Cornwall, Ontario, where a more modern mill was available. The company was able to make a little more profit, but the expense to the government of having to retrain those people, and the effects upon the economic and social life of the community in my opinion far outweighed that little extra money the company was able to make. That trend is continuing all the time.
I am glad to see that there is some hope in the maritimes, because the people are convinced that self help is the best thing. They have formed an organization which in my judgment will do much to reverse the trend and overcome this lopsided economic development we have today.
I see in the transportation improvements which have taken place, particularly in Nova Scotia, great possibilities of development in the future. We now have the Canso causeway which overcomes the bottleneck that existed in the movement of steel, coal and other products between the mainland and Cape Breton island. Then there is the ferry from North Sydney to Newfoundland which will help to develop interprovincial trade between that province and Nova Scotia, particularly Cape Breton island. There is also the bridge across the harbour from Halifax to Dartmouth, which will open up the eastern end of the province on the Dartmouth side. Then there is the Bar Harbor, Maine, and

Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, ferry. All these transportation improvements will bring about an improvement in industry and aid in the movement of our products.
In this connection something has taken place that should have taken place 30 years ago, the formation of the Atlantic economic council. It is all right to appoint royal commissions, but there have been dozens of them appointed. They simply write reports, most of them stereotyped, and you cannot get anything out of them; they are simply a rehash of the things that happened 50 years ago. But this Atlantic economic council is building up its membership and is gathering real facts.
In my judgment if in the years that lie ahead we can get a proper survey, if we can have proper planning in the utilization of the resources of the maritimes, if we can increase our interprovincial markets, which is the objective of the Atlantic economic council; if we can group those million and a half people into a market for the products of the maritimes and can save the millions of dollars which we pay in the way of protection for the manufacturers in central Canada; if we can utilize those savings in our own end of the country, these provinces can be selfsustaining. If the people really get behind those who are developing that Atlantic economic council these results will be achieved.
Until that time comes I think the federal government should co-operate with the provincial governments in that end of the country which are now doing some planning along the lines of self help in order to give them assistance or to take up the slack in areas where industry, like the mining industry, has gone out. A small defence industry employing 1,000 people would give great relief to the people of Nova Scotia if it were located there. I am sure that is equally true of New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island, but it is particularly true of the province I mentioned.

I am pretty sure that if Joe Smallwood of Newfoundland were given the opportunity to take in an industry he would find the means to do so.
I do not want to monopolize the time of the house in dealing with this particular subject, but it is one I have thought about quite a lot.

However, I should like to put on record some of the things that industry is doing along the lines of decentralization, in the constituency I have the honour to represent. I think we have some excellent examples there of what we might call forms of decentralization based on sound economic lines. In the vicinity of Edmonton we have had hundreds of millions of dollars invested


in industry during the past 10 years, in an area that was formerly the centre of a chiefly agricultural community. Of course some people will say, "You found oil and gas out there." We certainly did, and we are very happy about it. That is one of the main reasons for the industries that we have there today, but I suggest that is not the whole story.
We have several large oil refineries, and we have the terminals of two huge pipe lines, one going to the west coast and the other going to central Canada. But we have much more than that. At Edmonton we had a vast petrochemical industry established a few years ago. In other days we could visualize such huge industries being established only in the world's major cities, such as New York, Detroit or perhaps Montreal or Toronto, but now we have them in Edmonton. The combined investment in this type of industry alone runs to over $100 million, and expansion is still taking place.
Of course some people will say that is purely because oil and gas were found there, but I suggest there is more to it than that. We have also had established at Edmonton in the last very few years-less than five years-iron and steel mills, roofing mills and so forth. At the town of Fort Saskatchewan, which is located some 20 miles from Edmonton and has a population of about 2,000 people, we have a huge nickel refinery, and several other industries of a similar nature are planned there. That, in my opinion, is decentralization of the very best kind, where no government controls at all entered into the picture. There was no government interference of any kind. Industry has established itself there simply because it was economically wise and prudent so to do.
Then we have two pulp and paper mills projected for the Edmonton area, involving a capital investment of over $10 million. One of the pulp and paper mills is being built at a little place called Hinton, 180 miles west of the city of Edmonton. There again we have real and practical decentralization on a voluntary basis.
A little over a year ago a new cement plant costing over $12 million was started in the federal constituency of Edmonton West. It will be starting production this month. This cement plant in Edmonton West was no sooner begun than another company moved into Edmonton-Strathcona and now has near the production stage a second cement plant. Here again was no government direction, but the free play of free competition going full steam ahead in the development of this great country along sound economic lines. So I could

go on indefinitely. Other cities in Alberta are experiencing similar industrial activity, but on a somewhat smaller scale-Calgary, Red Deer, Lethbridge and so on.
Before I close I should like to emphasize this point. Those industries I have mentioned have sprung up at Alberta points since world war II because of very sound reasons. I am convinced that industry generally is keenly aware of the merits of decentralization. The captains of industry are not so slow; I think they have studied most of the points that have been brought up here this afternoon by hon. members. They know the values inherent in decentralization in this day and age, and I think they are not unaware of the fact that we are living in an atomic and hydrogen bomb age. But the captains of industry are also aware of the cost of decentralization. They have weighed, considered and evaluated all the factors concerned. They know there are many considerations other than merely decentralization for the sake of decentralization. I think we must go along with them a long way and recognize that the economic factors of the situation are very important.
Would any hon. member here suggest, for example, that there could be a paper mill established on Baffin island, just because it happens to be remote from our large cities? Where would the raw materials come from? Where would we get the power? Where would we find the workers for such an industry? Probably most important of all, where would we find the markets? How much would such an industry cost if it could be established in such a remote area, and who would meet these extra costs?

Decentralization of Industry sure that it is fraught with many dangers unless we take many other factors into consideration. Decentralization sounds fine, but without a little bit of economic sanity behind it, I believe it is largely a snare and a delusion. We simply cannot fly in the face of economic realities, as has been suggested here this afternoon.
I have nothing but praise for Canadian industry and what it has done so far toward decentralization. I believe decentralization is a good thing. I do not believe that all the industries in Canada should be concentrated in the central provinces. We in Alberta want all the industry we can get, and we are going out after it. The more that comes, the happier we will be. But I believe that we must be realistic about this thing. We could not possibly have deserved, shall I say, a petrochemical industry at Edmonton before the discovery of oil because it simply did not make economic sense.
As I have said, I am not opposed to decentralization of industry. For those areas which, like the one I have the honour to represent, have acquired new industries, we can assure hon. members here that it is a good thing indeed. But our industries have not been brought to Alberta by any kind of government direction. There were strong economic factors behind the new investments that have been made in our community. Without consideration of the economic factors we cannot get very far in the long run.
However, I am satisfied that we shall see more and more decentralization of industry in Canada in the years ahead as our country grows and develops and as new resources are discovered in the various parts of the country. I certainly hope that our good friends in the maritimes get their share. Nevertheless, I think we shall make a great mistake if we try to place on the statute books of Canada any legislation which will arbitrarily force industry to move from one part of the country to another.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the few moments that remain at my disposal tonight in the discussion of the matter of the decentralization of industry and its desirability, I should like to devote my attention particularly to the need for decentralizing industry. I think the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Lusby) gave a very good talk. I appreciated the way in which he approached the subject. As I recall it, he indicated to the house and the country quite clearly that it was impossible for us to have a really sound and flourishing Canada unless every part of
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Applewhaite).]

Canada is sound and flourishing. Consequently, what occurs in the province of Newfoundland is of vital concern to the province of Alberta and to every other province in the country and, therefore, what occurs in British Columbia or in any other province is of vital concern to the province of Newfoundland.
Little by little I can feel that hon. members, as each succeeding parliament convenes, are coming to realize this more and more, much more than they did in 1935 when I first came here. Bit by bit we Canadians shall begin to see that we must look after ourselves as a whole if we wish to go forward to the glorious destiny which all of us realize Canada can have.
How can this matter of the decentralization of industry be brought about? As I recall it, the hon. member for Cumberland quoted from a recommendation to the Gordon commission. If I am correct, four devices were outlined, as a result of the application of which we might render the decentralization of industry much more common and possible in Canada.
When I visited Britain in 1941 with the empire parliamentary association delegation, I was rather impressed to learn that Britain was divided into twelve regions for the purposes of the war, and each of those twelve regions, as I was informed, had a government of its own. Each had an industrial life of its own. Each had a military establishment of its own, so that in case all the other eleven were overcome by the foe the twelfth one could stand up and fight with all the power and vigour that it was capable of fighting with, with what remained of Britain.
Canada could very well aim at some such thing as that. As matters are now, I think we must all realize rather unhappily that if we get involved in a struggle and the industrial areas of Ontario and Quebec are seriously impaired it will greatly damage our fighting strength. If we were relying upon those two sources for our food and other supplies, and the enemy disrupted our transcontinental railways, it would put us at a tremendous disadvantage. We would be wise to give careful thought to all of this, and probably aim to make each province a selfsufficient emit as far as we can. I think the resources of the provinces are such that in the main that sort of ideal could be almost attained.
When we look at what has happened to the maritimes, as the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) pointed out so well this afternoon in that fine speech; when we look at the industries in the maritimes we

find that a most serious deterioration has occurred since they entered confederation. As hon. members will recall, the hon. member pointed out that 50 different industries had been siphoned off, as he said, from the maritime provinces into Ontario and Quebec. That might have been pretty good business for Ontario and Quebec, but it was bad business for the maritime provinces and in the long run it will be bad business for the two central provinces as well.
There are enough resources in this nation to support a population of many, many happy millions; but we shall never have the many, many happy millions so long as all the industry supporting this nation is concentrated in those two central provinces. Out in the other provinces there still is need of economic strength to support an adequate population.
What can we do about it? Well, let us examine for a few minutes the case of New Brunswick and see what happened to her as a result of entering the confederation of Canada. I hold in my hand the submission of the province of New Brunswick to the royal commission on dominion-provincial relations, issued in April, 1938. This submission is a most valuable document, because it undertakes to analyse for us what has happened to New Brunswick and what brought it about. Before I finish my remarks I may read some passages from this document, which, by the way, I commend to the most earnest consideration of every hon. member. First of all, 1 may say that New Brunswick attributes most of her ills to three main factors; an adverse tariff, which has injured her terribly; adverse freight rates, which have also injured her; and lack of control of credit.
If I may read from page 49 of the document, I think hon. members and the people of the country will be glad to hear these words:
The disadvantages from which New Brunswick has suffered in relation to the tariff were further accentuated and increased by the unauthorized burden of excessive freight rates on the railways in the maritime provinces after 1912.
May I interrupt there to recall what I was saying just before the house took recess. I said that all the federal government had done for Alberta up to the time the Social Credit government was elected in 1935 was to slap her in the face. One of the means by which she was slapped in the face was by the use of a most onerous and iniquitous set of freight rates, which it was positively a disgrace to foist upon any community whatsoever. The cost of getting goods out and the cost of getting our goods back were such that we hardly had anything left after those rates had been paid. Some of the most monstrous 67509-115

Principally as a result of these two elements industries became centralized in the province of Ontario and Quebec.
The two elements there were tariffs and freight rates. The submission continues: Large companies having their head offices in Ontario and Montreal bought up many industrial plants in New Brunswick and then closed them down. The manufacturing in New Brunswick at the present time is insignificant as compared with manufacturing in other parts of the dominion.
I do not know what was the matter with the federal government that they did not do something or other to try to stop the purchasing of those industries by these great concerns in Ontario and Quebec. It will be argued that this is a free enterprise country. I will grant that it is a free enterprise country. It is also a country which was organized under the British North America Act to see that every part of Canada prospered equally, and just as soon as the powers that were in Ottawa began to realize that that kind of thing was taking place something should have been done, but something was not done.

I do not think I shall have time to go into it tonight, so I shall have to discuss it at some later time, but certainly something ought to have been done. To say that something could not be done is simply to be utterly unrealistic and to acknowledge that the British North America Act, and Canada under that act, was a failure to begin with, which I am not ready to concede.
It goes on to say in the next paragraph:
In this connection it is well that the commission should bear in mind that the Canadian banks have been centralized in Ontario and Quebec. Prior to confederation and for some years afterwards we had our own banking institutions in this province and our people were able to obtain money for the encouragement of industry here.
I would think the very first matter of which the government in Ottawa would have taken cognizance was that very fact. Anyone with any intelligence whatsoever could see that if the banks of the maritime provinces came under the control of the banks in Ontario and Quebec, then the industries in the maritimes could be denied credit and could be seriously impaired if not destroyed, greatly to the immediate advantage of the industries in Ontario and Quebec, thereby rendering the maritimes practically vassal states to the two central provinces. It should not have taken intelligence of any high order

Decentralization of Industry to see that, and it should not have taken intelligence of any high order to have devised some means whereby that sort of thing could have been offset.
I do not hesitate to point out what I know every hon. member in the house readily recognizes, that unless we can remove the three disadvantages which the province of New Brunswick points out in the submission, as a result of which New Brunswick is faced with impossible odds, that province will never attain the greatness which she was designed by the Creator to attain. She will never be able to develop her resources and add fo her population, and she will never be able to be strong in that sense. She will always be a hewer of wood and a drawer of water, not because she has not the resources or the people willing to risk and toil, but because there is a paralysing force imposed upon her as a result of the indifference-or the cooperation, although I hope not the co-operation-of Ottawa.
What can we do? What the government needs to do and what the people of the country need to do, because we are all vitally interested, is this; find out what can be done in respect of these three matters and encourage people in the country to think about this matter. As I pointed out in a previous speech, there are altogether too many Canadians who view Canada with a snake's-eye view and not with a bird's-eye view, which soars aloft and sees the possibilities of this magnificent heritage which has been bequeathed us. There are possibilities not only for industrial strength but for increased population and over-all greatness arising from the loyalty of people who realize that they are getting a square deal and have a future worth looking forward to; that they can safely raise a family with assurance that the family is going to be able to have the means of supporting dignified and abundant lives. To say that such an ideal is impossible of attainment is to be utterly unrealistic, I maintain, and is tantamount to being a little Canadian instead of a big Canadian, a snake's-eye Canadian instead of a bird's-eye Canadian.
Let us now continue with the New Brunswick submission. The people who wrote the submission do not complain very much, but they do not pull many punches. On the same page it goes on to say:
The head offices of these hanking institutions were removed, after confederation, to Montreal and Toronto where they were situated more immediately in touch with the financial interests by which they were controlled.


Let us recall what the hon. member for Cape Breton South said this afternoon in relation to the picture which is indicated there. I quote the next paragraph of the submission'-
The result has been that industries in New Brunswick have not been able to obtain financial assistance in cases where such assistance would enable our local industries to compete with those in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec.
To what extent is that true today, Mr. Speaker? That is a question which must be asked and answered. We must also ask to what extent can we by actions in this parliament grant to New Brunswick the means of overcoming this handicap. I do not wish to go into financial matters in too great detail, but it is quite obvious that financial conditions go right to the very root of the matter.
I wish to put it on the record that I commend the hon. member for Edmonton-Strath-cona, for the very fine speech he made this afternoon, in which he expressed great understanding and appreciation and exactly the kind of ideals that Alberta people everywhere wish to express. But I point out that one of the great steps in giving Alberta a chance to get ahead was the treasury branch. The province of Alberta, exercising the powers given to her and Saskatchewan under their charter on entering into confederation, was able to lend money out of the treasury of Alberta, which meant that she was able to put at the disposal of the farmers and others in Alberta the credit of the province of Alberta as far as she possessed credit financially.
