speechtext: Even cabinet ministers.

subtopic: MOTION URGING ALL POSSIBLE EFFORTS TO PROMOTE DECENTRALIZATION
speechtext:
That is exactly what was demanded when we first put in the treasury branches. Then we had papers like the Calgary Herald and other big, wise know it alls beginning to complain how members of the legislature and cabinet ministers did not dare trust their money in the treasury branches. We had a campaign such as only those people can conduct; and members of the legislature and the cabinet, freely accepting the responsibility that was on them, began to do their banking business in the treasury branches thereby strengthening the treasury branches as a whole and the credit of Alberta so the farmers could produce more. What the members of the legislature did was to help Alberta to become strong, just as the people in a credit union help all the other people who are in the credit unions to be strong. This is plain common sense, and even a simpleton could understand it.
Very largely as a result of the treasury branches in Alberta the province was able to get a measure of control of her credit.

The bankers were not willing to lend in Alberta before the treasury branches were set up. An ordinary man in my district was not able to get a loan from a banker to save his life. The bankers turned up their noses and called common farmers uncredit-worthy. They said it was because the people were indebted, or for any one of a dozen other reasons. But as soon as the treasury branches were established in Cardston and Raymond and several other towns, the bankers came out on the street and buttonholed the men they had said were not credit-worthy before. The bankers were very ready to lend money to them then at 5 per cent, whereas before they would not have lent it at 8 per cent. I mention this just to show how potent was the effect on the Alberta economy of the introduction of the treasury branches. I submit that if we could build a set-up in the province of New Brunswick under which the province with the assistance of the dominion government, using Bank of Canada funds, could set up something comparable with the treasury branches of Alberta it would be simply astonishing how rapidly the economy of New Brunswick would begin to revive, just through a simple device like that.
There is one other thing worth considering. If it be that New Brunswick is too small a province, too insignificant to manage an important financial concern, then why not have New Brunswick and the other three Atlantic provinces combine their financial strengths? Let this Atlantic economic council, about which the hon. member for Cape Breton South spoke this afternoon, be given the power to establish financial means in the four Atlantic provinces as a result of the use of which they could begin to rebuild their economy. If that were done then we would find an immediate change for the better, which change would accelerate as the days went by, just as it has in the province of Alberta.
As I said a few minutes ago, there is simply no need for us to sit here and say that nothing can be done about this situation. There is no reason why we should be objects of contempt to such people as the communist leaders of Russia. There are plenty of producers in this country if we use free enterprise the way it could be used. We could then make Russia look like a nation of pikers. Let them do the best they can under their state ownership and socialism; we could do still better. What we lack in this country is not production, because we can produce until further orders.
That has been proved over and over again. We literally smothered our foes in two world 67509-1154
Decentralization of Industry wars with production, using private enterprise. The thing that on those occasions made it possible to use private enterprise to such advantage was that we then had the money with which the people could buy. That indicates quite clearly that it is a matter of finance. To say that we cannot devise means in this country whereby we can make our financial instruments the servants of our productive instruments is to prove ourselves unworthy of being where we are. I read further from page 50 of this report:
Pertinent cases may be cited where local industries in this province have been destroyed because of the difficulty of financing and we submit that finances have been withheld as local industries might come into competition with similar industries in the last mentioned provinces.
I appeal to all hon. members. Can you think of a more hopeless position in which a group of people could be than that in which the province and the people of New Brunswick found themselves under circumstances like that? At the same time you have people boasting all over the place about free competition. There was not anything resembling free competition under those circumstances. New Brunswick could no more compete freely with industries in Ontario and Quebec than a man could compete with a wrestler when he had both hands tied behind him. There is one suggestion I make as to how we can overcome the disadvantage which confronts us.
There is further discussion to be found on page 63, but I have not time to go into that because my time is practically exhausted. This indicates how the tariff was used to choke off and destroy the fish canning industry of New Brunswick. I wish I had time to read all that will be found on page 64. They set out a number of little technicalities, rules and devices which permitted the tariff to be used to place difficulties in the way of this great industry which represented an investment of $2 million, and it was practically ruined. I am not sure whether it had to close its doors.

subtopic: MOTION URGING ALL POSSIBLE EFFORTS TO PROMOTE DECENTRALIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate, first of all I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Brandon-Souris for moving this resolution. I think he has raised a question which is important and timely. With the principle that the government should encourage the decentralization of industry I have no quarrel whatever, but the practical application of that principle is another matter. I hope to be able to consider that further on in my speech.
There is perhaps no need for me to remind the house that there are many economic factors governing the localization of industry with which this whole question is intimately bound up. First there is the question of the availability of raw materials. Second, there must be an available and adequate supply of skilled labour. Another essential is the proximity to large markets, and here I am thinking not only of the actual number of consumers composing the market but the purchasing power possessed by those consumers. We know that if a demand is to be effective it must have purchasing power. Another indispensable factor is cheap and efficient means of transportation, and another is a plentiful supply of power at reasonable rates.
To these important economic factors perhaps two more might be added, namely an adequate supply of capital and an adequate supply of managerial ability. However, these are much more mobile factors and respond more quickly to the magnet of the other factors, particularly the movement of capital which naturally gravitates through the sensitive mechanism of the money market to those areas in which it can be employed to the best advantage.
It is obvious that for all these reasons some areas are better endowed by nature than others to become great industrial centres. It is hard to resist the pull of natural advantages, and indeed it is not always desirable to attempt to do so. All through history economic and geographical factors have powerfully influenced the location of industry, and in


our own time modern technological developments have contributed to industrial concentrations.
I should like to turn now to the problems that arise out of the centralization of industry, especially when that centralization becomes excessive. First of all, undue centralization of industry militates against a wider and more even distribution of prosperity throughout any country. Second, it causes a drain on labour skills and business ability from the periphery to the centre of the country. I have often heard it said that the Atlantic provinces have been threatened with the loss of some of their best brains to other parts of Canada. This movement of population imposes a heavier burden on those who remain. A single example might perhaps suffice to illustrate this point; the per capita cost of provincial services immediately rises.
Another aspect of this problem to which I think we might devote a few moments is that it is a self-perpetuating process. The exodus to the centre swells the mass market, for instance, of central Canada, thereby increasing the advantages of industrial location there. At the same time it produces precisely the opposite effect in the peripheral provinces. In a sense it is a vicious circle, with cumulative effects that are very serious to the lesser industrialized provinces. Then again, it causes population congestion in the great metropolitan centres, with certain social and moral disadvantages to which various hon. members, including the mover of the resolution, have drawn our attention and upon which it is unnecessary for me to dwell at any length. Certainly it makes great problems for municipalities in such matters as juvenile delinquency, traffic difficulties and so on.
In my opinion one of the most important aspects of this question is the strategic aspect. We all know that we are living in a thermonuclear age and that nuclear air attack, if it comes, which God forbid, will cause heavy casualties in our populous centres. The incidence of these casualties will be all the greater because of congestion of urban centres. Then too, from the standpoint of the effect of such attacks upon the country's economy, that economy is undoubtedly rendered more vulnerable by undue centralization of industry. If a country's industrial centres are knocked out, the entire economy can be paralysed because the flow of goods to the rest of the country will dwindle to a trickle or perhaps even cease altogether. Wider dispersal would mitigate this problem.
Undoubtedly Canada has the great advantage of wide spaces, and it seems to me that

this advantage should be utilized to the utmost that is practicable. What I have said particularly applies in the case of defence industries which, of course, are all-important in war. We do not want to be faced with a situation in which the fighting strength and power of resistance of the country may be knocked out by a few terrible blows on great industrial centres. It is my view that the problems of civil defence-and we know they are very grave and very complicated- are aggravated by undue centralization of industry.
The problem of industrial centralization has, in my opinion, particular relevance to my own province of Newfoundland. Here the impact of industrial centralization is felt by both the consumer and the producer. Newfoundland has derived great benefits from the union with Canada. That is recognized very clearly in Newfoundland, particularly as regards social services; but I should like to point out that there is another side to the picture.
Prior to confederation the Newfoundland consumer could buy in the cheapest markets. Now this freedom has been circumscribed to some extent by the Canadian tariff system. Here I should like to refer to a few figures concerning the distribution of Newfoundland's external trade before union, when separate statistics were kept. In the year 1947-48, for instance, Newfoundland exported to Canada goods to the value of $11 million, but imported from Canada goods to the value of almost $55 million; so that even before confederation the mainland of Canada enjoyed a favourable trade balance with Newfoundland by almost five to one. Since confederation, although no official figures are available, there can be no doubt that sales from the mainland of Canada to Newfoundland have greatly increased. An estimate by one competent source has placed them at about $150 million. That, of course, is unofficial, but I think it is a fairly accurate estimate.
Of course there has been a marked diversion of Newfoundland purchases since union from other countries to the mainland of Canada, particularly from the United States. Unfortunately, however, there has been no corresponding increase in Newfoundland sales to the mainland of Canada. That is perhaps inevitable in the economic circumstances, for the mainland and Newfoundland economies are competitive rather than complementary.
This is particularly true in the case of two of Newfoundland's three staple exports, namely fish and newsprint. The only important exceptions are iron ore and, to a lesser degree, fluorspar.
Decentralization of Industry
It will not have escaped the notice of the house, I know, that recently the provincial government of Newfoundland, under the dynamic and imaginative leadership of Premier Smallwood, to whom I was glad to hear the hon. member for Cape Breton South pay such a handsome tribute earlier in this debate, has undertaken a bold program of industrial development. New industries, some 16 in number, have been established with government assistance and under government sponsorship, though not under government management. Some of those industries look to the Newfoundland market; others to the mainland markets. Sales in the Newfoundland market benefit the Newfoundland consumer and help to some degree to offset the disadvantages of centralization of industry.
Sales to mainland markets are, however, handicapped by distance. Newfoundland is at the end of the line, on the extreme east coast. It is, of course, a maritime province in the sense that it is an oceanic province, an island province. Low coastal shipping rates are essential to the Newfoundland consumer and producer alike. We must have low-cost shipping facilities. The keenest possible competition among shipping services is necessary in order to keep down shipping rates.
Here I feel I must refer to a matter which is giving very great concern to Newfoundlanders at the present time. That is the attempt of certain mainland shipping interests to exclude ships of United Kingdom registry from Canadian trade. This exclusion would be fatal to Newfoundland. I cannot overemphasize that fact. It would be really a death blow to the island's economy. It should be borne in mind that the only other means of transportation of goods into and out of the island is by means of a narrow-gauge, single-track railway which is greatly overburdened at the present time.
Another aspect of this situation to which I should like to draw the attention of the house concerns its fiscal effects. Newfoundland's contribution to the federal treasury is, I believe, much greater than it might appear at first sight, because of the sales made in Newfoundland of goods produced on the mainland of Canada. Federal excise tax and federal sales tax are paid on those goods produced on the mainland and sold in Newfoundland, but when the taxes come into the federal treasury they come not from Newfoundland but from the provinces of the origin of the goods.
Then also I think it is important to point out that a considerable part of the corporate income tax paid by mainland companies on manufactured goods sold in Newfoundland and personal income tax paid by employees

Decentralization of Industry of all ranks in these firms are, to some extent, due to the sales made of these goods in Newfoundland. That, of course, is true also of other provinces which are consuming centres for the great industrial regions of our country.
As has been pointed out by the hon. member for Cumberland who, I thought, made a most admirable contribution to this debate, there are practical limitations on the role which the federal government is able to play in this matter of encouraging the decentralization of industry. First of all there are the constitutional limitations of our federal system. Second, there are the economic limitations imposed by economic laws operating within the private enterprise system. Both these systems, in my opinion-that is the federal system and the private enterprise system-are essential to the development of our country.
It is true that this framework imposes certain unavoidable limits upon the opportunities with which the federal government is presented to encourage decentralization. Nevertheless, I believe that even within this framework there are steps which can be taken by the federal government. Of course these have been taken, and they have contributed in large measure to the development of the provinces in all parts of the country. I am confident that these steps will continue to be taken by the government which has done so much to promote the prosperity of the nation as a whole.
Amongst these I would single out for special mention the maintenance of equitable freight rates; co-operation with provincial governments in scientific surveys of natural and industrial resources, particularly in the underindustrialized areas of the country; and the placing of government orders, where these are possible and economical, with firms operating in underindustrialized areas.
I offer these comments in no merely provincial spirit but from the standpoint of Canada as a whole. In this great country of ours the prosperity and the well-being of the whole are inextricably bound up with the prosperity and the well-being of all the parts. The optimum development of the industrial resources of every province of Canada is in the best interests of the Canadian nation as a whole.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have the opportunity to take part in this debate, but only for a brief period, I hope, because I realize it is an important one and that' there are many other hon. gentlemen who want to take part in it. The day is a rather short one

because of the fortunate circumstance at 2.30 this afternoon, when we had the opportunity of greeting the head of the Italian state. I therefore intend to speak but briefly. In fact, however, I should like to speak for a long while.
One sometimes gets disturbed-I will not say irritated-by what one hears. This afternoon I thought suggestions were made- perhaps it is oversensitiveness on my part

that some people were a little bit worried about the maritime province or felt that the maritime provinces were making some special plea on this occasion. Actually, Mr. Speaker, that is not the case, and I think all of us from the maritimes rather resent any such implication. I almost caught that suggestion, I thought, from the remarks of the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona, who said he did not think anything could be done by legislation and that nature would have to take its course.
After all, some of us remember the fact that before they joined confederation, the maritime provinces happened to be the most prosperous section of what was then the Dominion of Canada, and that some parts of Canada which now boast of their wealth were occupied only by Indians. Sometimes we almost wish they still were, to be a little bit facetious about the matter. Certainly the natural resources about which they boast today were part of the natural heritage which we assumed was being taken over by the provinces which at that time formed confederation. At any rate, whatever may be the accident of geography today, the fact remains that in those eastern provinces there was a remarkably high degree of prosperity. After confederation that prosperity-to put it mildly and to use a conservative understatement-did not maintain the same relative position.
I realize that there are historical reasons for that fact. In the first place, just before confederation there was the civil war and the great prosperity which the maritime provinces enjoyed through being able to ship goods to the United States. I almost think one could be frank and say that they shipped goods to both sides over the border during that conflict. There was also the fact that the great wooden shipbuilding industry, which had flourished in the maritimes, had given us a predominance in trade not only with what was then Canada, the eastern provinces and British North America as such, but also in trade all over the world.
Of course, shortly after confederation came the economic development of the steel ship and wooden ships passed out of commercial

practice and practicality. It may be-and I think possibly the criticism can be fairly levelled-that in the maritime provinces, particularly in Nova Scotia, an effort should have been made to shift from wooden ships to steel ships, to maintain the position which we theretofore had occupied. But whether or not that is a fair criticism, the fact remains that the shift was not made. As a result, shortly after confederation the relative prosperity of the maritimes lapsed and we did not keep pace with the rest of Canada. I am also prepared to admit that in the maritimes sometimes there has been too much of a habit of placing one's head on the shoulder of confederation and weeping over the ill effects of confederation upon the maritime economy.
I think we have overplayed that, frankly.
I think, to a large extent, it was political. After all, confederation became a political issue in our province. The Liberals were opposed to it. They fought it and they carried all the maritime governments against it after confederation and, in fact, once before it. When prosperity slipped away, whether it was their fault or whatever the reason, there was a natural tendency to say, "Well, didn't we say confederation was a bad thing." Then all the maritime governments began weeping on the shoulders of confederation; it became a provincial policy to place the blame largely on confederation. That is part of the background of this feeling which we sometimes hear suggested, as we did this afternoon, that we have overemphasized the disabilities which we have suffered.
Whether or not that was justified in the past, it is not for me to say. But I can say this. I think the maritimes have tried to accomplish something despite some of the obvious disabilities from which they suffer. This is not the place to discuss it. When the estimates of the Minister of Transport are before us one could take a full 30 minutes in that committee, then continue after an interruption for another 30 minutes, speaking on the freight rate structure and the disabilities which have been imposed upon the maritimes because of it.
When we entered confederation we were told, it is true, "You are not going to be able to ship to the south. You are not going to be able to enjoy the trade pattern which you have enjoyed heretofore. But there is going to be an east-west pattern developed, and you are going to profit immeasurably by that." The Intercolonial Railway was built for that purpose. Up until 1911 or 1912, before the outbreak of world war I at any rate, that pattern was fairly well maintained.

Notwithstanding that, Mr. Speaker, there are firms in the maritime provinces which have maintained a national position, and not only those in the luxury trades such as confectionery. For instance, the hon. members for Halifax have one great national firm there, and there is another one in New Brunswick. Despite all the difficulties of the textile industry, that industry in Nova Scotia is still maintaining a national position. There are the heavier industries such as Enterprise Foundries at Sackville, which manufactures stoves and furnaces, amongst the heaviest articles manufactured today. They are still maintaining, either by good management, by ability or by fighting against this adverse trend, a national position. There are many other firms in the maritimes which have done likewise. As the hon. member for Cape Breton South suggested this afternoon, it is true that many have disappeared. On the other hand, there have been at least some which have been able to maintain their position.
The situation in the maritimes has not been one of stagnation. It has been one of development, but our complaint is that relatively the development has been, I will not say immaterial but at least not in keeping with the developments that have taken place in other parts of Canada. I just happened to be glancing over a report of the Nova Scotia Light and Power Company. We have a public utility commission in Nova Scotia, and we have a large privately owned utility. There are also two or three smaller ones. When you glance over that report you notice that during the last five years the output of electricity by this firm has been doubled. It has been trebled since the war and they are envisaging doubling it again in the next seven years, and again doubling it in the following seven years. They do realize that there is development taking place in the maritimes, particularly shall I say in Nova Scotia.
If one looks at the population figures one sees that our population in that province increased by 11-2 per cent between the two censuses of 1941 and 1951. I notice, and I am sure the Halifax members are proud of this fact, that the population of the city of Halifax has increased between 1941 and 1951 by over 35 per cent. It has only been exceeded by four other cities in Canada, the four western cities of Edmonton, Calgary, Vancouver and Victoria. We are not, therefore, in
1816	HOUSE OF
Decentralization of Industry a position of weeping on someone's shoulder. We are not sitting here crying at the moon, and we are not saying that the situation is hopeless or that nothing has been done. We are appealing to the government to help us.
Our people there have tried to help themselves. I should like to say of the Nova Scotia Light and Power Company, to which I referred a moment ago-I am sure the hon. member for Cape Breton South would support me in this if he were here-that instead of using oil in its generating plant, as it could have done being situated at Halifax, it has installed steam generating plants using Nova Scotia coal for the development of that steam, thereby increasing the use of Nova Scotia coal. If their plans are carried out for doubling and redoubling the output in the next 14 years, there will be a tremendous increase in the use of Nova Scotia coal by that one plant alone.
As I have said we have tried to do, and I think we are doing, something to counteract this situation which developed following confederation. As the hon. member for Cape Breton South said this afternoon, I think the organization of what is briefly called APEC, or the Atlantic provinces economic council, is a forward step. We believe it will have a marked impact on the development of the maritime provinces. You now have the four Atlantic provinces, not just the maritime provinces but the four Atlantic provinces of Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, associated in one economic council with a secretariat and staff organized to make studies of the problems with which we are confronted and attempt to arrive at some solution on a common basis. I am quite sure when that economic council, financed by three Liberal governments and one Conservative government at the moment, make their recommendations they will not accept the suggestion that was made this afternoon that there is nothing the federal government can do to assist in carrying this into effect. I believe there is.
As I said, whatever developments we have made-and I emphasize this because sometimes I think the suggestion is that we have done nothing for ourselves-nevertheless it is the relative position which disturbs us. I should like for a moment to give one or two figures with respect to that. I am speaking now of the three maritime provinces. In 1949 we had 9-2 per cent of the total national population. By 1954 that had dropped, not terribly but nevertheless it dropped, from 9-2 per cent to 8-7 per cent. Our percentage of labour employed had dropped from 8-3 per cent in 1949 to 7-5 per cent in 1954. Perhaps most important of all, Mr. Speaker,
[Mr. Nowlan.l

the percentage of new investment and capital investment had dropped from 6-5 per cent to 4-8 per cent, which is a very substantial drop in new investment.
In so far as Nova Scotia itself was concerned, I could not get the figures for the maritimes for 1954, but I did check with the dominion bureau of statistics this afternoon and they gave me these figures for the percentage of new investment and capital investment in Nova Scotia in 1950, as 3-7 per cent. In 1955, last year, it had dropped to 2-8 per cent. In this connection it should be pointed out that our manufacturing investment dropped over 24 per cent between 1949 and 1955. In other words, Mr. Speaker, the 2 [DOT] 8 per cent of the national investment which we had in 1955 was largely represented by institutional investment, hospitals, schools, plus investments made by the Minister of National Defence in enlarging national defence organizations in the maritime provinces and in Nova Scotia.
As I said, when you see that our manufacturing proportion dropped 20-3 per cent, despite the fact that in other parts of Canada it increased tremendously, you can understand that we are somewhat concerned about the situation. If it had not been for the investments made by the Department of National Defence in their installations-not in productive facilities such as factories-at Shearwater, at Stadacona, at Greenwood in my own constituency, and at Cornwallis in my own constituency, and all over because of our geographical position, because we happen to be one of the provinces on the eastern seacoast which has to be prepared for whatever emergency may come, we would be in a worse position. Because of our geographical location we have had this tremendous expenditure in national defence installations, which accounts almost entirely for the new capital investment which has taken place in the maritimes. It has accounted for almost all of the new capital investment which has taken place in Nova Scotia during the last few years.
We all know, Mr. Speaker, or we all hope, that this type of expenditure will not be permanent; that it is something based on an emergency, and it is not productive except for the moment. Because of the enlarged barracks and the increased and enlarged installations we of course get the wages and salaries of the personnel and their purchases, and it all contributes to an expanding economy. But when the time comes, as we hope it will, that these expenditures can be restricted, then the economy of the maritimes

vis-a-vis the rest of Canada will be even worse than before these expenditures were made.
When you see the briefs which have been filed with the Gordon commission-I am not going to read the figures which were given this afternoon-which show that over 80 per cent of all of the industrial development is taking place in the two central provinces; and when you envisage all this great further development which is going to take place along the St. Lawrence river basin and in southern Ontario, I do not think those of us who come from the maritimes can be criticized if we suggest that something should be done to reverse this trend and try to make national production more widely distributed in this country.
The hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona said, "Well, you cannot of course do this by legislation". No one is suggesting, at least in this resolution, that it can be done by legislation, but legislation can accomplish something. I did not hear him objecting in the last three weeks when we were discussing legislation which was certain to be of benefit to some parts of Canada, Mr. Speaker.
We have on the order paper legislation which presupposes the expenditure of some millions of dollars for the construction of a pipe line, which will be of assistance to some parts of Canada but certainly not to the maritime provinces. We have had on the order paper and in the estimates hundreds of millions of dollars for the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway, which certainly is not going to benefit the maritimes; in fact, it is going to be an absolute deterrent to them in every way, shape and form, and that legislation was perfectly acceptable. I do not think there were any shudders or any nausea when it was passed.
I can say this. The members from the maritime provinces support that legislation because we believe in Canada, and we want to see a strong Canada developed, even stronger than that which we have had heretofore. But we do believe a national policy works both ways. A national policy should not be created to make only a strong centre, which we perhaps are a little bit envious of but which we accept. We also believe it should be extended to the periphery of this country as well.
Today we heard something about the constitutional problem; that constitutionally this parliament cannot do anything. But, Mr. Speaker, the constitutional problem is greater in the United States than it is here because, if I remember my constitutional history and constitutional law at all, in the United States
Decentralization of Industry the residuary power is vested in the individual states, and only delegated powers are vested in the central government, whereas our position is the reverse.
Well, what do we find in the United States? We find that country has been able to pass legislation and to offer tax exemptions, for instance, to industries which will locate in certain states, giving certain inducements so far as freight rates are concerned to industries which will locate in certain states. The President has directed national defence industries to locate in certain states. These are three steps which have been adopted and carried into practice by the United States of America. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, if that can be done by that country with their constitutional problems, then the same thing can be done by our country where the constitutional problem is far less.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South spoke this afternoon about the steel industry and what could be done there. We all believe this in the maritimes, Mr. Speaker: the thing which made us prosperous in the past, and which made us great, really-and we were great; we were small but we were great provinces-was the fact that we had an export position. We could take part in international trade, and we were able to ship to the markets of the world.
We still have that export position. You cannot tell me that with a steel plant such as we have in Nova Scotia, or such as could be developed there, the Minister of Defence Production or this government could not direct that more of those products could be made in Nova Scotia or in the maritimes so they could be shipped more economically to our NATO allies and to other parts of the world. There are scores of things such as this that could be done.
I am not going to elaborate further because I made a promise to myself that I was not going to speak so long as to interfere with the half a dozen others who I am sure want to speak, but I do say in conclusion there are things the government could do. There are certain constructive measures that could be taken either by freight rates, by taxation, or by the allocating of industries, and probably in more ways. If we had the time, if we had two or three days in which we could debate this, I would like to make further constructive suggestions with respect to it. But I do say that I heartily approve of this resolution, and I believe that every hon. member should approve it. We are all proud of Canada; we are all proud of the fact that we are Canadians, but we do believe, those of us from the periphery, that something along that line should be done.

Perhaps those from the west coast, because they have been blessed by Providence with greater wealth and natural resources than we have been blessed with in the east, do not suffer from the peripheral position to the same extent we do; but this country can never become the country that the fathers of confederation envisaged unless we develop a national policy which will make all parts of Canada relatively prosperous. It is not that we expect the 80 per cent of the industrial development, or anything of that kind. But I know, I am convinced, that steps can be taken to rectify this trend which has developed here, not during the last few years but for many years. The time has come when it must be rectified; I believe it can be. subtopic: MOTION URGING ALL POSSIBLE EFFORTS TO PROMOTE DECENTRALIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the resolution introduced in the house this afternoon by the hon. member for Brandon deserves another reading for the information of the hon. members. It is as follows:
That, In the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of taking advantage of every possible opportunity to promote the decentralization of industry, particularly with reference to defence industry, thereby,
(1)	helping to reverse the trend towards concentration of population in large metropolitan areas with the accompanying social evils;
(2)	encouraging a more equitable distribution of population and development right across Canada, and
(3)	assuring the strategic dispersal of vital war industries in the interests of national defence.
The principle of that resolution or motion presented by the hon. member is perhaps very commendable, but we are indeed surprised that the opposition should put forward such a resolution since it amounts to inviting the government to implement a regimentation policy which has long been denounced by the Liberal party. We would understand a motion like this being introduced by a socialist group, such as the C.C.F. party but coming as it does from a Progressive Conservative member, it surprises the house.
Of course only an authorized spokesman of the Progressive Conservative party can present such a motion in its name. This new stand in favour of regimentation can only be explained by the fact that his party has never, for more than a quarter of a century, put forward a clear-cut policy as far as the


economic and social welfare of the Canadian population is concerned.
A few weeks ago, we witnessed a tragedy on the T.V. screen when the young representative from Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer), proud of his membership in the Progressive Conservative party and in his capacity as chairman of the national association of his party, was utterly unable to state the Progressive Conservative policy in answer to questions put to him by newspapermen on behalf of the Canadian population.
It is therefore not surprising that the house was astonished this afternoon to hear a member speak in favour of a policy of regimentation because but a few months ago, in fact last July, the official spokesmen of the Progressive Conservative party emphatically opposed certain powers that parliament proposed to grant to the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce and of Defence Production (Mr. Howe).
Industrial decentralization consists in using regimentation to uproot certain industries established in the industrial provinces of Quebec and Ontario, and forcing them to establish themselves in other provinces, following a survey of the industrial situation throughout Canada, from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
Tonight I would like to state the views of western Canada, and more particularly those of Manitoba. I believe that the policy so well shaped by the Liberal government of Canada has, everywhere and at all times favoured industrial decentralization because, after all, even in Manitoba, during the war, we witnessed the departure of a large number of our young people and heads of families who enlisted to defend their country. Others went to work in industries established in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario; in spite of all that, many Canadian citizens came to settle in the western provinces and particularly in Manitoba.
Since the great victory of the allies in 1945, numerous industries have established themselves in Manitoba, where an imposing number were already operating. For instance, in my own city of St. Boniface we have the largest stockyards and packing plants of the British Empire, while in greater Winnipeg there are large textile, clothing, sugar beet, cement and other industries. Since 1945 more than 500 new industries have been established, a fact which has enabled the people of western Canada to receive each month a large amount in the form of salaries. The establishment of these industries has obviously contributed to the economic advancement of the Canadian nation.

Salaries in western Canada packing plants are in excess of $14 million. I wonder if the hon. member for Brandon would not be the first to protest, if the government were forced, as a result of this motion having been carried, to require, for instance, the packing plant in Brandon to remove to Portage la Prairie, shall we say, so that the people of that community could be allowed to enjoy the economic benefits accruing from such a plan. Yet, that would just about be the policy which would follow upon the passage of that motion.
I do not think we should adopt that motion since the Liberal government, after all, ever since it came into power back in 1935, has taken all possible steps necessary towards improving the economic and social well-being of the Canadian people.
As regards decentralization, may I point out that industry has always been encouraged along that line by legislation introduced in this house and now placed on our statute books.
The report of the industrial development bank indicates that it has on numerous occasions extended financial assistance to those Canadian citizens who wished to establish industries in western Canada. We might add too that the National Housing Act has made possible the building of a great number of houses in western Canada. All that has brought constant benefits to the Canadian people. These are but two instances of beneficial legislation enacted by the Liberal government. Such legislation is abundant. With the support the Canadian people has always given the Liberal government, I am sure that we will be able to keep on improving the economic standards of our country, which makes the envy of all the other nations of the world.
I am opposed to such a motion because it would mean the enforcement of an act of regimentation which, as I stated a moment ago, is inconsistent with the policy of the Liberal party. Moreover, through the increase in population in western Canada, and the establishment of industries in always increasing numbers and through the help of the minister of industry and commerce of Manitoba,-who has done everything in his power and has even appointed a foreign representative to find ways and means of bringing new industries to western Canada, all that with the support of the federal government- western Canada will soon enjoy constant prosperity in the industrial sphere. I would rather
Decentralization of Industry support a policy of steady economic progress, such as we have always enjoyed since the Liberal government came to power in 1935.
The beneficial steps taken not only by the provincial ministers of western Canada but especially by the federal Liberal government were meant to ensure the progress of the agricultural industry which has steadily improved not only under the right hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) but in particular under the direction of the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce. I am sure that but a small minority among Canadians, during the depression, would have been ready to burn them in effigy and that, with the present economic and social development going on throughout the country, the Canadian people are willing to erect a monument to these ministers. All this is due to their knowledge of our problems and of course to their desire of forever upholding the great principles of the Liberal party.
Mr. Speaker, these are the few remarks I wished to make tonight. I am sure that what we want is to maintain our policy which has been so firmly established for a long time and to reject any legislation conducive to regimentation.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to take only a few minutes this evening to discuss this resolution. The resolution is quite familiar to me, because I have heard similar resolutions moved in the house a number of times. I want to congratulate hon. members who have spoken already, particularly the hon. member for Brandon-Souris, who moved the resolution, and the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, who spoke of the situation in the maritime provinces. As a matter of fact it was such a splendid speech and illustrated our position so well that I feel it is hardly necessary for me to say anything. I want to thank the hon. member for Lethbridge for taking up the cudgel on behalf of my own province of New Brunswick.	.
This subject has been debated in the house on many occasions. I remember in the late thirties when it was brought up. Then during the second world war we asked that industry be decentralized and different sections of the dominion given a share in the production of war materials. We brought up the matter
1820	HOUSE OF
Decentralization of Industry during the so-called cold war and requested that the outlying sections of Canada, such as the maritime provinces and certain sections of the west, be given some opportunity to produce war materials. Even now we do not consider it is too late for the government to give consideration to this important problem.
It has been pointed out that with industry concentrated in great centres like Montreal, Hamilton and Toronto, in case of an attack, if such a thing should happen, the country would be in a very poor position indeed. Our war industry could be entirely destroyed without much effort on the part of the enemy.
Despite the fact that these matters have been discussed in this house for many years, what is the net result? As has been so well illustrated by speakers here today, I think it can be said that the net result is that there is more industry today in Quebec and Ontario than there ever was before. The people of the maritime provinces and other parts of Canada who were poor before are today poorer, while the people in the central part of Canada are richer today. That is a state of affairs which we hoped would be corrected.
It is not necessary to go back into history to the days of confederation, because those days are past and gone and we must look to the future. To review the situation which has existed in this country for 80 years is not going to help us. Of course we can tell how in 1871 New Brunswick had 10 per cent of the industry of this country while its population was not 10 per cent of the whole. There was hardly a village or town in any part of New Brunswick or the maritime provinces that did not have its small industry. The economy was well balanced, the people were happy and contented, and they stayed in their own part of Canada.
As the hon. member for Cape Breton South has said, today Ontario has 49 per cent of the industry of Canada, Quebec has 33 per cent, while New Brunswick with a population of practically half a million has only 2 per cent of the total industry of Canada. Such a situation is not healthy, and I feel it is one which should be corrected.
The sad deterioration of our position during past years can be blamed, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Lethbridge, upon certain things. Let me say to the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona that the government does have something to do with this. As was pointed out by the hon. member for Lethbridge, an adverse tariff is one of the reasons why the maritime provinces have lost their industries. That is something over which federal governments, not provincial governments, have had complete control since confederation.
[Mr. Brooks.l

The hon. member referred also to adverse freight rates. The federal government has complete control of freight rates. The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings referred to the lack of control over credit, which is a matter under the control of the federal government. There is another item which could be added to the list mentioned by the hon. member for Lethbridge. This did not apply in days past, but it has applied for the last 20 years. I refer to the lack of cheap electrical power in those provinces.
I should like to quote the remarks made by a former premier of the province of New Brunswick, Hon. J. B. McNair, who is today the chief justice of our province, during the dominion-provincial plenary conference of 1945. Referring to the situation in his own province he had this to say:
Let it be remembered again that the control of all matters national in their scope and which affect most vitally the social and economic well-being of the people in the provinces is now vested in the central government. I have already mentioned the main items. The chronic unbalance in the Canadian economy with the heavy concentration of industrial, commercial and financial power in certain favoured areas, is due to the play of forces under the control of the dominion parliament and government since confederation. That situation is capable of being remedied, and only remedied, through national policy.
That was the opinion of the premier of New Brunswick, a very able man, as expressed in 1945, and it is the opinion of the people of New Brunswick today and has been the opinion of the people of the maritime provinces since confederation. As I said before, that opinion has been expressed repeatedly to governments in this country, but today the situation is no better, in fact it is even worse than it was 25 or 30 years ago.
During the second world war billions of dollars were spent, but only one-half of one per cent was spent for the development of industry in New Brunswick. As the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings said, we were there down by the sea with the great ports of Halifax and Saint John, with people willing and ready to work, yet industry was concentrated in the central part of Canada and the products had to be carried over railroads which were frightfully congested during that period in order to reach those ports. No effort was made at all to create war industry in the maritime provinces.
Then there were the after-effects of the war. During a debate in this house at the beginning of the war I suggested that we should have more manufacturing in the maritime provinces of the requirements of war. The then minister of fisheries, Hon. Mr. MARCH 5. 1956
Michaud, said, "We do not want to manufacture too much in New Brunswick; the result will be that we will have a lot of empty factories in the maritime provinces after the war is over."
There were a lot of empty factories after the war was over. Where were they? They were in Quebec and Ontario. They were sold to commercial concerns at fire-sale prices, and today they are going concerns employing tens of thousands of people. If we had had some industry in the maritime provinces in those days, I believe today we would have industries flourishing in that part of the country. That was one way in which this federal government at that time could have helped the people of the maritimes.
I do not wish to take up a great deal of time, as most of the points have been covered. But this question of decentralization is not new in Canada, and it is not new in other countries of the world. The hon. member for Lethbridge mentioned the fact that they have decentralized war industries in other countries. They have not only decentralized their defence production indus-dustries, but they have decentralized other industries. In Paisley, in Scotland, they are establishing atomic energy reactors, so that part of the British Isles may be productive as far as industry is concerned.
I remember that some years ago the British government said that Durham was in a depressed area, and that it would start some industries there in order to make it as economically sound as other parts of Great Britain. The same thing was done in Wales. In southern United States years ago were producers of cotton, which they sent to the northern part of that country. As producers of the cotton for the north they were simply hewers of wood and drawers of water, but that situation was changed. The federal government and the Tennessee valley authority realized that those people would become great industrialists if they had cheap power in that part of the country. Cheap power was given them, and today the southern states have become greatly industrialized and they are not the poor section of the United States.
From 1919 to 1939 the New England states lost 40 per cent of their industries and 25 per cent of their working population. The people of those New England states said that something must be done, and in 1939 an effort was made to get more industry for the New England states. The great textile factories were bought up and used for other purposes, with the assistance of the federal government at Washington. Today there is a great improvement in the situation in that
Decentralization of Industry part of the country, owing to government policies. I have here an article in the Christian Science Monitor of January 16, 1956, which
says:
Today, New England industries are producing an amazing array of products used in nuclear installations and equipment throughout the country.
They are doing that through the atomic energy commission. It also says:
Similar defence department contracts have served to spur New England's leading industry: aviation.
It goes on to say that today, with the impact the government has given to that part of the United States, industry is in better condition there than it was many years ago. The Christian Science Monitor also speaks of decentralization in the matter of defence production, in an article dated December 28, 1955:
Production Shift Set
. . . air force secretary Donald A. Quarles laid down the policy Dec. 28, approved by the defence department, reversing the old idea of building up war industries after the start of hostilities.
The main paragraph, which I shall call to the attention of the house, reads as follows:
Mr. Quarles stressed the need for dispersal of war industry but emphasized that vulnerability was the key consideration and that dispersal is one factor in reducing vulnerability.
That is a statement by a very able man, and it is a statement that should well be taken into serious consideration by the government in this Dominion of Canada. A good look should be taken over this dominion, and industries should be given to the parts of the country I have mentioned.
Mr. Speaker, you may ask us how you could help the province of New Brunswick. The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings very aptly told us different ways in which the government could help. I and other members from New Brunswick have on many occasions here in the past few years told how our province could be helped without any cost to this dominion. What we need to encourage industries and to bring industries to the east is cheap power. I was surprised to hear the hon. member for Cape Breton South say they had as much power as they needed in Nova Scotia. I rather question that, because I read not so long ago that Nova Scotia could have had a $10 million pulp and paper mill in the southern part of that province if it could have had cheap power with which to operate.

subtopic: MOTION URGING ALL POSSIBLE EFFORTS TO PROMOTE DECENTRALIZATION
speechtext:
In speaking on this resolution I am sure that I will be expressing, in greater or less degree, the views of every member of this house. I suspect, however, that there
Decentralization of Industry are many different ideas on what decentralization means. A town a hundred miles from Toronto or Montreal compares its relative position with that of one or other of these great cities, and a sigh is emitted, touched perhaps, as was said this afternoon, by envy. In Nova Scotia or in the far west we must sigh much more loudly in order that the sound may carry the necessary distance to Ottawa, or what should be more important, to the point of the concentration of private enterprise industry in the upper provinces. That perhaps accounts for the superior lung power of those from the provinces more distant from the centres of larger population.
I am concerned mainly with decentralization of industry that will encourage a more equitable distribution of population and development right across Canada. In our private enterprise economy the government cannot instruct or direct industry to locate in any particular spot. The choice of a location for a plant involving the expenditure of any substantial amount of money is usually made after careful consideration of all the factors that will affect the cost of doing business. That is good, sound logic. A firm weighs the risks and then takes the plunge. Except in a few rare instances, competition is such that it must scratch pretty hard to make things go; at least that applies in the maritimes. Most Canadians feel that the responsibility for such decisions should rest with the firms, and that in the long run this will bring the greatest good, in a material sense, to the greatest number.
The government does not direct industrial location, nor can it by legislation endow an area with resources, eliminate distances by act of parliament or remove the tariffs and other obstacles to trade put up by other countries. What then can it do to encourage a more equitable development across Canada? When confederation took place the greatest single problem confronting the individual provinces was the cost of providing adequate transportation facilities. This is still the most important single factor affecting the development of Nova Scotia's economy today. Distance from the central Canadian markets on the one hand and tariff barriers in our export markets on the other have us in a very tight squeeze.
For this reason I urge upon the government the need to maintain and extend its efforts to reduce trade barriers. If we are to sell fish, lumber, wheat, base metals, we must accept goods in return. We cannot have our cake and eat it. Our people demand a high

The government has more direct control over transportation costs as they affect the outlying provinces. Speaking as a Nova Scotian I have said before in this house, and I urge again, it is time we took another look at the Maritime Freight Rates Act. There is no need for me to go into the history of this legislation and its application. It is sufficient to refer to the relative position of the steel industry in Nova Scotia compared with its competitors in Ontario. In public statements the president of Dosco has said that since the war the freight rate on steel bars to the main industrial market in Canada has practically doubled, while for one of its competitors the increase was less than 10 per cent and for the other roughly 60 per cent in the same period.
This is only one example, but it is enough to show that unless some action is taken the relative position of the Atlantic provinces will deteriorate rather than improve with the growth of Canada. Many factors have contributed to this; the growth of highway transport to the more populous areas, horizontal rate increases, and so on. While the freight picture is worsening, other more encouraging things have happened. Progress has been made on the trans-Canada highway; air travel facilities have been steadily improved; the national harbours have been greatly developed. All in all, our transportation facilities have come a long way.
The most important single development in this field in recent years has been the St. Lawrence seaway. Some years ago, in 1950 to be exact, when this project was still in the planning stage, I asked what study the government had given to the economic effects of this undertaking. In particular I was concerned that due attention should be given to the possible ill effects the seaway might have on certain maritime industries. I should like to be assured that some responsible federal agency has been given the responsibility for continuous study of this matter. This aspect of the project should be regarded as a national responsibility, and it should not be just left to the provinces to point out the difficulties. If as much effort were put into this as is going into research on how to keep the St. Lawrence river open the year round, we would be very happy.
The government is to be commended for the work it has initiated in the provision of

research facilities. The national research council in Ottawa and its maritime regional laboratory in Halifax are an imaginative effort for regional service. The provision of vocational and trade training in conjunction with the provinces has been important to industry in Nova Scotia. This is true of the fisheries as well as manufacturing generally, and the construction industry. Perhaps most important of all is the possibility of developments in atomic energy which will be available to all parts of Canada, irrespective of location. This is a field in which federal development should pay off for all provinces in equal measure.
We are, of course, interested in obtaining defence industry, but in particular we are interested in privately owned industry. Defence industry may be a temporary matter. You build up a locality with defence factories, then the pressure is off and they close leaving many people unemployed. We are interested in holding what we have. As so many speakers have said tonight, since confederation we have lost many industries. In particular, Halifax has lost several. There was a time in 1867 when we had many English distributing houses. They have all gone and are now found either in Montreal or Toronto. We had several cigar factories. They are all to be found today submerged in some upper Canadian plant. We had a broom factory, and we had shoe factories. In time they were sold to those industries in Upper Canada. Recently we have all received letters from the boot and shoe industry, particularly the rubber footwear industry, concerning importations from Hong Kong and what they are doing to the industry here. It was just that sort of thing that happened in Nova Scotia over the years.
Then at the time of the Halifax explosion there was a cotton factory which was blown up. What did they do with the money they were paid as compensation? Did they put it into another factory at Halifax? No; that also went to Montreal. Then on the east side of Halifax harbour, in Dartmouth, there was a very fine industry which closed.
May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
